messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 77
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Surgeon
- Trauma Type: Witnessed other trauma
- Pcl5: 56

He is a 77-year-old South Eastern Asian man who has spent most of his life in surgery, a profession that taught him to stay precise, controlled, and useful when others are in pain. He is married now, and his wife remains a steady presence in his life, but there is a part of him that still seems to live in the operating room of decades ago, in the moment when he first witnessed trauma he could not repair.

He recalls the event as if it happened yesterday, though it occurred early in his career, when he was still eager to prove himself and still believed that skill and discipline could protect him from the worst things medicine would show him. He was called in after a violent incident, and the body he saw before him was not his patient in the ordinary sense, not someone he could prepare and guide through an elective procedure, but a person damaged by forces outside anyone’s control. He remembers the smell, the blood, the urgency in the room, and the helplessness that settled into him as he realized that careful hands were not enough. What stayed with him most was not only what he saw, but the feeling that his own body had become strangely absent, as though he were moving through the scene from a distance while another version of himself kept working.

Afterward, he went back to work. That is how he has always dealt with things: by returning to duty, by tightening his focus, by refusing to be distracted by what is unbearable. For years, he told himself that the event had been simply another hard day, one more tragic case among many. Yet over time, the memory began to intrude in ways he could not fully predict. In the operating room, the scent of antiseptic sometimes gives way, for a second, to the older smell he associates with that scene. A sudden cry from a patient or a family member can make his chest go tight and his hands feel unsteady, even now. He notices that he scans rooms unconsciously, as if part of him is still looking for danger before it arrives.

He is proud of the life he built, but he also lives with a strict inner discipline that can make him seem distant. His wife says that when he is troubled, he becomes quieter rather than more expressive. He does not often speak about the past, especially not about the traumatic scenes from his training and career. When conversations drift near that subject, he changes the topic or becomes formal, almost clinical. There are nights when sleep does not come easily. He lies awake replaying images he has spent years trying not to name, and when he does sleep, it is not unusual for him to wake with a start, disoriented and irritated, as though pulled suddenly back into his body from some unsafe place.

He also notices that he has become less patient with reminders of suffering. News reports, dramatic television, even certain stories from younger colleagues can make him feel unexpectedly tense and restless. At times he avoids them altogether. He chooses routes, routines, and environments that feel predictable. He likes order and dislikes surprises, and those preferences have sharpened with age. He still works with care and remains deeply competent, but he experiences a private cost: the effort it takes to keep himself composed. Underneath that composure is a persistent sense that the world can turn violent without warning, and that he is never entirely free from the old image.

As he talks about it now, there is a sadness in him, but also a kind of weary acceptance. He does not describe himself as broken. He describes himself as someone who learned early to carry what he saw and keep going. Yet even in that stoicism, there are moments when the memory presses in and his face changes, when he grows still and distant, and the room seems to narrow around what he cannot forget.
